extra.message: Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization of HTTP Request Body — Full remote code execution; attacker sends crafted pickle payload as the HTTP body and achieves arbitrary code execution with application process privileges. [verified: This is the same pickle.loads() deserialization issue as idx 1 — pickle.loads(raw) on the raw HTTP request body. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 1.]

Remote Code Execution via eval() with User-Controlled Expression — Full remote code execution on the server; attacker can read/write arbitrary files, exfiltrate secrets, pivot to internal network, or achieve complete system compromise. [verified: This is the same eval() issue as idx 2 — eval(expr, {'__builtins__': {}}, ...) with user-supplied expr; the empty-builtins sandbox is bypassable via CPython object MRO traversal. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 2.]

Server-Side Template Injection via User-Controlled Jinja2 Template — Full remote code execution via Jinja2 template sandbox escape; attacker can execute arbitrary Python code and OS commands. [verified: This is the same SSTI issue as idx 3 — Template('Result: ' + fragment).render() with user-controlled fragment. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 3.]

OS Command Injection via Unsanitized host Parameter — Arbitrary OS command execution with the privileges of the application process; attacker can exfiltrate files, install backdoors, or pivot to internal services. [verified: This is the same os.system() command injection as idx 5 — _os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host) with unsanitized user-supplied host parameter. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 5.]

OS Command Injection via Unsanitized `host` Query Parameter — Remote code execution as the application process user. Attacker can execute arbitrary shell commands, exfiltrate data, install backdoors, or pivot to internal network. [verified: os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host) concatenates the unsanitized host query parameter into a shell command; shell metacharacters like ';', '&&', '|' allow arbitrary command execution. Gated only by _wrk_gate static token with no sanitization.]

SSN and Credit Card Numbers Written in Plaintext to Filesystem — Any filesystem access (backup exfiltration, path traversal, server compromise) yields plaintext SSNs and PANs; PCI-DSS non-compliance; regulatory and legal exposure. [verified: The vault endpoint writes user-supplied SSN and card number fields to disk as plaintext JSON with json.dumps; no encryption or masking is applied, violating PCI-DSS requirements for cardholder data protection. This is also compounded by the path traversal vulnerability in ref.]

Path Traversal in SSN/Card Write Endpoint + Sensitive Data Written to Disk in Plaintext — Arbitrary file write via path traversal. Additionally, SSN and payment card numbers supplied by the caller are written to disk in plaintext JSON — sensitive PII exposure at rest. [verified: BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f'{ref}.json' uses an unsanitized ref from query params or request body then writes plaintext SSN and card data to the resulting path; ref='../../etc/crontab' traverses outside the base directory. Additionally, plaintext PII (SSN, card number) is written to disk unconditionally, violating PCI-DSS.]

Jinja2 |safe Filter Applied to User-Controlled Input — If rendered in HTML context, user-supplied content bypasses Jinja2 auto-escaping and enables stored/reflected XSS. [verified: This is the same XSS via |safe filter issue as idx 14 — Template('{{ card|safe }}').render(card=card) with user input returned as HTMLResponse. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 14.]

CORS Origin Reflection with Credentials Allowed — Any attacker-controlled website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint on behalf of authenticated users, enabling CSRF and cross-origin data theft. [verified: This is the same CORS origin reflection issue as idx 11 — the dispatch_origin_mirror_569 endpoint reflects the Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, bypassing the global CORSMiddleware restrictions and enabling cross-origin credentialed requests from any attacker-controlled origin.]

Hardcoded 4-Digit Region Authentication PINs — Attackers can authenticate as any region (north/south) by brute-forcing the 4-digit PIN space or by reading it from the repository, gaining access to region-scoped dispatch operations. [verified: known = {'north': '4812', 'south': '5930'} hardcodes 4-digit region PINs in source code; they are visible to anyone with repo access, are only 4 digits (10,000 possibilities with no rate limiting), and cannot be rotated without redeployment — all constitute genuine hardcoded credential weakness.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Write via User-Controlled Filename — Attacker writes arbitrary content to arbitrary filesystem locations writable by the process; can overwrite cron jobs, SSH authorized_keys, or application config files for persistence or privilege escalation. [verified: This is the same path traversal / arbitrary file write as idx 4 — BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name with unsanitized user-supplied name. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 4.]

Reflected XSS via Jinja2 |safe Filter on User-Controlled Input — Reflected XSS in the ops panel. An attacker can craft a URL that executes JavaScript in the browser of an ops admin viewing the endpoint, stealing session cookies or performing actions on their behalf. [verified: Template('{{ card|safe }}').render(card=card) applies the |safe filter to a user-supplied card query parameter and returns it as HTMLResponse; the |safe filter bypasses Jinja2 auto-escaping, so any HTML/JavaScript in card is rendered verbatim in the browser, enabling reflected XSS against ops users.]

XXE Injection via lxml with DTD Loading and Entity Resolution Enabled — Attacker can read arbitrary local files (including /etc/passwd, environment files, SSH keys) and make server-side HTTP requests to internal services. [verified: This is the same XXE issue as idx 7 — lxml XMLParser with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False parsing the raw request body. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 7.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Write via Unsanitized `name` Query Parameter — Arbitrary file write as the application process user. Can overwrite application source code for RCE, write SSH authorized_keys, cron jobs, or overwrite database credential files. [verified: BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name uses pathlib's / operator with unsanitized user-supplied name query param, then calls target.write_bytes(body); pathlib does not prevent traversal when the component contains '../' sequences, so name='../../etc/cron.d/backdoor' resolves outside the base dir. Gated only by _wrk_gate static token.]

NoSQL Injection via User-Controlled MongoDB Query Filter — Attacker can bypass query filters and exfiltrate arbitrary documents from the MongoDB ops database, potentially including sensitive operational records. [verified: This is the same NoSQL injection as idx 8 — user-supplied JSON body passed directly to MongoDB find_one() as the query filter. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 8.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection via lxml with Full Entity Resolution and Network Access — Server-Side Request Forgery and arbitrary local file read via OOB exfiltration. Can leak /etc/passwd, application secrets, database credentials, and make internal network requests. [verified: etree.XMLParser(load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False) with the raw request body enables classic XXE; an attacker can send a DOCTYPE with SYSTEM entity referencing file:///etc/passwd and, with no_network=False, exfiltrate data OOB via external HTTP. Gated only by _wrk_gate static token.]

Wildcard CORS with Credentials Reflection — Attacker-Controlled Origin Reflected — Cross-origin requests with session cookies from any attacker-controlled domain. Enables CSRF-equivalent attacks and cross-site data theft against authenticated ops users. [verified: origin = request.headers.get('origin', '*') is reflected verbatim into Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; this is the classic CORS misconfiguration allowing any attacker-controlled origin to make credentialed cross-origin requests. The global CORSMiddleware only restricts localhost origins for the main app but this endpoint sets its own response headers overri]

Plaintext Password Reset Token Exposed in API Response in Non-Production Environments — Account takeover for any known email address. Attacker triggers password reset, reads token from response, and immediately resets password without email access. Bypasses the entire email verification step. [verified: The code confirms `if APP_ENV != 'production' and dev_token: response['dev_reset_token'] = dev_token` and the default APP_ENV is 'local' per .env.example, meaning every non-production environment (staging, QA, demo) returns the raw reset token in the unauthenticated API response, enabling full account takeover for any known email without email access.]

Password Reset Token Returned in HTTP Response — Unauthenticated account takeover for any account on non-production deployments (staging, QA, beta, local); attacker obtains raw reset token directly from the API response. [verified: Same finding as [0] at a slightly different line reference: `response['dev_reset_token'] = dev_token` is returned whenever `APP_ENV != 'production'`, with default `APP_ENV=local`, enabling unauthenticated account takeover on any non-production deployment — confirmed duplicate of finding [0].]

Hardcoded Default API Key in Seed Data — An attacker with knowledge of the hardcoded key can authenticate to the integration endpoint and manipulate job statuses across all regions (the seeded key has no region_id restriction). [verified: The hardcoded key 'fd_demo_status_key_please_rotate' is inserted verbatim by seed.py with region_id=None, no environment guard, and no rotation mechanism; any attacker with the public source can immediately use it against a seeded deployment. The SHA-256 hash storage provides no protection since the exact plaintext is in source, and the /api/integrations/status-update endpoint requires only this k]

Hardcoded Credentials in Frontend JS Bundle — Attacker fetches the JS bundle, reads working credentials for all four user roles including ops_admin, and gains full authenticated access to the application. [verified: Lines 167-170 hardcode working credentials for all four user roles (admin, dispatcher, worker, customer) all using 'DemoPass123!' as onClick quick-fill values that are shipped in the public JS bundle. Any unauthenticated visitor can fetch the JS asset, read the email/password pairs, and authenticate as any role including ops_admin without any additional barrier.]

Sensitive Data Written to Logs (Request Body and Authorization Header) — Credential and secret exposure in log files. Authorization tokens or bearer credentials logged in plaintext are accessible to anyone with log file read access (log aggregators, SIEM, sysadmins). [verified: logger.warning('route manifest intake body=%s auth=%s', wire_text, request.headers.get('authorization')) logs the full request body and raw Authorization header value to application logs; any party with log access can harvest bearer tokens or API keys from those logs.]

Open Redirect via Unvalidated `lane` Query Parameter — Phishing attacks against ops personnel. Can be combined with SSRF if used in server-side redirect following. Can bypass referrer-based access controls. [verified: RedirectResponse(lane) returns the user-supplied lane query parameter directly as the redirect URL with no validation; an attacker can pass lane=https://evil.com to redirect ops users to attacker-controlled sites for phishing. The gate restricts this to callers with the ops token, but the redirect is still exploitable by token holders or via SSRF chaining.]

TLS Certificate Verification Disabled for Outbound HTTPS Requests — Man-in-the-middle attacker on the network path can intercept and modify all outbound HTTPS traffic from this endpoint; sensitive data transmitted to external services is not protected. [verified: This is the same TLS verification disabled issue as idx 13 — ssl._create_unverified_context() used for outbound HTTPS. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 13.]

TLS Certificate Verification Disabled for Outbound HTTPS Request — Man-in-the-middle attack on outbound HTTPS. Attacker on the network can intercept traffic, inject responses, and steal any data sent to the partner endpoint. [verified: ssl._create_unverified_context() disables TLS certificate verification for the outbound HTTPS request; an on-path attacker can intercept and modify the HTTPS traffic to partner.invalid without detection.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints (Login, Registration, Password Reset) — Brute-force password attacks against any account. Dictionary attacks against the login endpoint can compromise accounts with weak passwords. Registration can be abused for spam/enumeration. [verified: Code review confirms no rate-limiting middleware (no slowapi, no custom throttle), no account lockout, and no per-IP attempt tracking anywhere in the codebase; the login, registration, and password-reset endpoints are fully open to unlimited automated requests, enabling brute-force and enumeration attacks.]

Plaintext Password Reset Tokens Written to Log File — Account takeover via log file access. All reset tokens are stored in plaintext in a predictable path, allowing credential harvesting by anyone with filesystem access. [verified: The code confirms `handle.write(f'{datetime.utcnow().isoformat()} {user.email} token={raw}\n')` writes every plaintext reset token to `local_mocks/password_resets.log` with no environment guard, accumulating all tokens indefinitely and exposing them to any process or system with filesystem read access (log shippers, backups, compromised process).]

Session Cookie Missing Secure Flag on Registration Endpoint — Session token theft via HTTP interception (passive network attacker, shared Wi-Fi, HTTP downgrade). Attacker captures session cookie and hijacks newly registered user sessions. [verified: The register endpoint hardcodes `secure=False` while the login endpoint correctly reads from `os.getenv('COOKIE_SECURE', 'false')`, meaning any operator who sets `COOKIE_SECURE=true` in production still receives an insecure session cookie from the `/register` endpoint, transmitting the token over plain HTTP.]

Password Reset Tokens Written to Log File in Plaintext — All active password reset tokens exposed if log file is accessible; enables account takeover for any user who has requested a password reset. [verified: Same finding as [1] at a slightly different line reference: plaintext reset tokens are written to `local_mocks/password_resets.log` with no environment guard, accumulating all tokens indefinitely — confirmed duplicate of finding [1].]

Session Cookie secure=False Hardcoded on Registration Endpoint — Session cookie transmitted over plain HTTP on registration; network attacker can intercept the cookie and hijack the newly-created session. [verified: Same root cause and code location as finding [2]: the register endpoint hardcodes `secure=False` while login uses the COOKIE_SECURE env var, causing session cookies to be transmitted over HTTP even in production deployments that set COOKIE_SECURE=true — this is a confirmed duplicate of finding [2].]

Session Cookie Missing Secure Flag on Registration Endpoint — Session cookies issued at registration are transmitted over plain HTTP, enabling network attackers to steal session tokens via passive eavesdropping and hijack user sessions. [verified: Same finding as [2] and [8]: the register endpoint hardcodes `secure=False` on the session cookie set_cookie call, ignoring the COOKIE_SECURE environment variable — confirmed duplicate of findings [2] and [8].]

CSV Formula Injection in Export Endpoints (Incident/Route/Completion Reports) — When ops staff open exported CSV files in spreadsheet software, attacker-injected formulas execute, potentially exfiltrating data via DDE/formula callbacks or executing OS commands (via older Excel DDE). [verified: User-controlled fields (`customer_summary`, `internal_notes`) are written directly to CSV rows via the csv_response helper with no formula-injection prefix sanitization (no stripping of =, +, -, @), so a malicious customer can inject spreadsheet formulas that execute when ops staff open the exported CSV in Excel or LibreOffice.]

CSV Formula Injection in Incident/Route Export Endpoints — When an ops-admin opens the exported CSV in Excel or Google Sheets, attacker-controlled formulas execute, enabling data exfiltration, phishing, and potentially RCE on the analyst's workstation. [verified: Same root cause as finding [5] at a different export endpoint (line ~1441 vs ~716): user-controlled fields written to CSV without formula-injection sanitization; if this is a distinct endpoint (export_incidents vs another export), both require the same fix — confirmed duplicate or co-instance of finding [5].]

Webhook HMAC Signing Secret Stored in Plaintext — A database dump, backup compromise, or SQL injection attack immediately exposes all webhook signing secrets, allowing permanent forgery of signed webhook payloads to all integrated downstream systems without any key rotation being possible. [verified: backend/app/models.py line 311 defines `WebhookEndpoint.secret` as a plain `String(120)` column, and main.py stores it verbatim (`secret=payload.secret`) with no hashing or encryption, in direct contrast to `ApiKey` which applies `hash_secret()` before storage. Any database read access (backup leak, SQL injection, compromised admin) exposes all webhook signing secrets in cleartext, enabling perman]

CSRF Token Stored in localStorage (Stealable by XSS) — Any XSS on the origin can steal the CSRF token from localStorage and the session cookie is sent automatically, enabling full CSRF bypass and account takeover. [verified: Line 53 reads the CSRF token from localStorage and lines 80/157 write it there; localStorage is accessible to any same-origin JavaScript, so an XSS vulnerability anywhere on the origin can read the CSRF token and combine it with the auto-sent session cookie to make fully authenticated state-changing requests, completely bypassing CSRF protection.]

Hardcoded Default Password in Admin User Creation Form — Any attacker who knows the default password can immediately authenticate as any admin-created account where the password was not changed, gaining unauthorized access to the platform. [verified: Line 567 initializes the AdminUsers form state with `password: 'TempPass123!'`, a publicly-known default that is visible in the open-source repository; any admin who creates users without changing this field produces accounts with a shared predictable password, allowing unauthorized access to those accounts by anyone who reads the source code.]

Hardcoded Default Webhook HMAC Secret — Attackers with repo access can forge webhook HMAC signatures to bypass signature verification on any downstream system integrated via webhooks created with the default secret. [verified: Line 935 (AdminIntegrations) initializes webhook state with `secret: 'local-demo-secret'`, a hardcoded default HMAC signing secret visible in the public repository; if an admin creates a webhook without changing this value, any attacker with repo access knows the signing secret and can forge valid HMAC-signed payloads to any downstream webhook consumer that trusts this secret.]

Sensitive Path Information Leaked in Error Response — Information disclosure of internal filesystem paths, aiding path traversal and file write attacks on the ops endpoints. [verified: RuntimeError(f'failed to import {lot_ref} from {BASE_EXPORT_DIR}') is returned verbatim in the JSON error response, leaking the absolute BASE_EXPORT_DIR path to any caller with the ops token; this aids in constructing precise path traversal payloads for other endpoints.]

XSS Protection Headers Explicitly Disabled by Endpoint — Browser XSS auditor and CSP protections are disabled for responses from this endpoint; combined with any reflected content, XSS exploitation is fully unrestricted. [verified: This is the same security headers removal as idx 12 — X-XSS-Protection set to '0' and Content-Security-Policy cleared. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 12.]

Security Headers Disabled (CSP Cleared, XSS-Protection Disabled) — Removal of browser-side XSS defenses. Any XSS vulnerability in the application becomes more exploitable in browsers that respect these headers. [verified: The endpoint explicitly sets X-XSS-Protection: 0 and Content-Security-Policy: '' on its response, removing browser-side XSS defenses for that response. While X-XSS-Protection is deprecated in modern browsers, clearing CSP on an HTML-returning endpoint that could contain user input has measurable security impact.]

Debug/Trace Endpoint Exposes Environment Variables and Filesystem Paths — Disclosure of APP_ENV setting and export directory path. Aids attackers in understanding the deployment environment and crafting targeted attacks. [verified: The trace endpoint returns os.environ.get('APP_ENV') and str(BASE_EXPORT_DIR) to any caller with the ops token, disclosing the deployment environment name and exact export directory path that can be used to target other vulnerabilities.]

Environment and Filesystem Path Disclosure via Trace Endpoint — Attackers learn the server's deployment environment (production vs. dev — enabling or disabling dev-mode features like plaintext reset tokens) and the absolute path to the export directory for precision path traversal attacks. [verified: This is the same environment/path disclosure issue as idx 16 — the trace endpoint returns APP_ENV and BASE_EXPORT_DIR to callers with the ops token. Confirmed true positive and duplicate of idx 16.]

IP Spoofing via Unvalidated X-Forwarded-For Header in Audit Logs — Attackers performing unauthorized actions can forge their IP address in audit logs, completely falsifying the forensic trail and preventing attribution after a security incident. [verified: The `client_ip()` function reads `X-Forwarded-For` and returns `forwarded.split(',')[0].strip()[:64]` with no trusted-proxy validation, allowing any client to forge an arbitrary IP in audit log entries; since no IP-based access controls exist in the codebase, the confirmed impact is audit trail integrity corruption only.]

User Account Enumeration via Registration Endpoint — An attacker can enumerate which email addresses have accounts by attempting registration. This enables targeted phishing, credential stuffing, and harassment of known users. [verified: The registration endpoint returns HTTP 409 with `'An account with this email already exists'` for duplicate emails, while login correctly returns the same message for both wrong-password and missing-user cases; an unauthenticated attacker can enumerate all registered emails via this asymmetric disclosure.]

Account Enumeration via Registration Endpoint — Attackers can enumerate valid email addresses registered on the platform, enabling targeted phishing, credential stuffing, and social engineering attacks against known users. [verified: Same finding as [4]: the registration endpoint returns HTTP 409 with an explicit 'email already exists' message, enabling unauthenticated email enumeration — confirmed duplicate of finding [4].]

Client-Supplied Content-Type Stored and Served on Proof Download — Stored XSS / content-type confusion. If a victim downloads a proof with a manipulated content-type, browser may render HTML/JS from the file. Limited by ALLOWED_UPLOAD_CONTENT_TYPES check, but text/plain is allowed and could contain HTML rendered by some browsers. [verified: The upload endpoint stores `file.content_type` (client-supplied) verbatim in the DB and the download endpoint serves it back as `media_type=proof.content_type` in FileResponse; while `text/html` is not in ALLOWED_UPLOAD_CONTENT_TYPES preventing direct XSS, the client fully controls the Content-Type header served to downloading users, enabling content-type confusion and latent XSS if the allowlist ]

Insufficient Tenant Scoping on Incident Update (IDOR Risk for Cross-Region Dispatchers) — A dispatcher with no region assigned (`region_id=None`) can update any incident across all tenants/regions. Cross-tenant data modification. [verified: The `update_incident` handler fetches by PK and raises 404 before performing the authorization check, creating an existence oracle where any authenticated user (including ROLE_CUSTOMER) can distinguish non-existent incidents (404) from existing-but-unauthorized incidents (403), leaking valid incident IDs; the cross-region dispatcher access (region_id=None) is intentional design, not a bug.]

Insecure File Upload — Client-Supplied Content-Type Trusted Without Content Validation — Attackers can upload arbitrary file types (HTML, SVG, scripts) disguised as allowed MIME types. If the upload directory becomes web-accessible or files are served with user-controlled Content-Type, this enables stored XSS or drive-by downloads. [verified: The upload_proof endpoint validates only `file.content_type` (client-supplied multipart header) against ALLOWED_UPLOAD_CONTENT_TYPES with no magic-byte inspection of actual file content, and `application/octet-stream` is explicitly in the allowlist, meaning any binary file can be uploaded regardless of actual content; the impact is limited since the download endpoint requires auth and FileResponse]
